extracted.intended_audience: school administrators, higher-education and K-12 officials, and legal counsel responsible for Title IX compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory preamble and legal guidance accompanying the Department of Education's final Title IX regulations, describing definitions, interagency interactions, procedural standards, and case-law-informed enforcement expectations for recipients and commentators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'pregnancy or related conditions'
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble uses the terms “pregnancy or related conditions” and “pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions” interchangeably to mean any condition covered under the definition of “pregnancy or related conditions” in final §106.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department clarifies interchangeable usage and points to the regulatory definition in §106.2 for the exact scope of conditions covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential employee vs. confidential resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters used 'confidential resources' to encompass non-employees; the final regulations' term 'confidential employee' only covers employees of a recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or drafting policies, distinguish between non-employee confidential resources (as commenters sometimes meant) and the regulatory term 'confidential employee', which is limited to employees. Use the term consistently with the regulation's intended scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction between Title IX and FERPA (GEPA override)
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is a direct conflict between the requirements of Title IX and FERPA, the GEPA override, as incorporated into §106.6(e), applies such that a recipient must comply with Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies and practices should be designed recognizing that Title IX obligations may supersede FERPA when a direct conflict exists, pursuant to the GEPA override in §106.6(e); see the preamble discussion of §106.6(e) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction between constitutional due process and FERPA (constitutional override)
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is a direct conflict between constitutional due process rights and FERPA, a constitutional override applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must give precedence to constitutional due process protections over FERPA where a genuine direct conflict exists; the preamble and the discussion of §106.6(e) elaborate on this interplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERPA right to inspect witness statements that are directly related to the student
rubrics_metrics.description: Under FERPA's definition of education records, 'a parent (or eligible student) has a right to inspect and review any witness statement that is directly related to the student, even if that statement contains information that is also directly related to another student, if the information cannot be segregated and redacted without destroying its meaning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools must be prepared to provide access to such witness statements when segregation/redaction would destroy meaning; the Department cites prior guidance and case examples (e.g., video of hazing) illustrating this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of treatment records to postsecondary/adult students (FERPA treatment-records rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may choose to disclose a treatment record for a postsecondary student or a student who is eighteen years of age or older to that student, and that treatment record would then become an 'education record' under FERPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should be aware that voluntary disclosure of treatment records to eligible students converts those materials into education records, with the attendant FERPA obligations and rights, per the Department's prior Dear Colleague guidance referenced in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak Out Act effect on nondisclosure/non-disparagement clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speak Out Act, 42 U.S.C. 19403, generally prohibits the judicial enforceability of a nondisclosure clause or non-disparagement clause before a dispute arises involving a sexual assault or sexual harassment alleged to be in violation of Federal, State, or tribal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions and contracts should be reviewed in light of the Speak Out Act; pre-dispute enforcement of NDAs/non-disparagement terms concerning alleged sexual assault/harassment is generally barred under federal law as explained in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate indifference may require intensified/responsive action
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a recipient's response to sex discrimination is assessed under the deliberate indifference standard in a private action for damages, some courts have recognized that the recipient must take additional responsive action if its initial efforts to end sex discrimination are ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited (e.g., Cianciotto, Doe v. Sch. Dist. No. 1) show courts denying dismissal where complaints alleged failure to 'intensify, reassess, or adjust' responses; institutions should plan escalating/responsive measures if initial interventions fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'participation in the Title IX process' (retaliation context)
rubrics_metrics.description: References to participation 'in the Title IX process' include contexts where a person 'reported information, made a complaint, testified, assisted, or participated or refused to participate in any manner in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing under this part, including in an informal resolution process under §106.44(k), in grievance procedures under §106.45, and if applicable §106.46, and in any other actions taken by a recipient under §106.44(f)(1),' consistent with the definition of 'retaliation' in §106.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing retaliation claims or drafting retaliation protections, use this broad definition of 'participation' to determine protected activity, and ensure policies reference §106.2 and the listed processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling of cross-complaint/counter-complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters referred to a filing as a 'cross-complaint', though the Department notes that this type of complaint is sometimes referred to as a counter-complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The label (cross-complaint vs. counter-complaint) does not alter the functional treatment under Title IX procedures; institutions should be clear about how they process responsive filings regardless of the label used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination and 'fundamental fairness' in disciplinary hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Some courts have held that fundamental fairness requires, at a minimum, that the university provide a way for people accused of sexual misconduct to cross-examine witnesses, directly or indirectly, at a hearing where the witnesses appear in person or by other means; other courts have rejected that extension and courts generally require only a basic/fundamental fairness standard in the absence of constitutional protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes conflicting case law (e.g., Doe v. Allee vs. Boermeester) and advises readers to consider the prevailing constitutional protections; private institutions should adhere to 'fundamental' or 'basic' fairness but be aware of differing circuit and state precedents regarding cross-examination rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to counsel in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: As stated in Haidak, there is generally no right to counsel in disciplinary proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should recognize that courts commonly hold there is not an automatic right to counsel in school disciplinary contexts; policies can permit counsel but are not constitutionally required in most contexts, subject to applicable law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum comment-period expectation for substantial rule changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When substantial rule changes are proposed, a 30-day comment period is generally the shortest time period sufficient for interested persons to meaningfully review a proposed rule and provide informed comment (citing Nat'l Lifeline Ass'n v. FCC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulewriters and agencies should treat 30 days as a general floor for meaningful public comment on substantial changes; shorter periods risk procedural challenge and are rarely adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA/retroactivity principle for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: 5 U.S.C. 551 defines a 'rule' as an agency action with 'future effect'; Bowen holds that a statutory grant of legislative rulemaking authority will not, as a general matter, be understood to encompass the power to promulgate retroactive rules unless that power is conveyed by Congress in express terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should avoid retroactive regulatory effects unless Congress clearly authorizes them; preambles should analyze retroactivity carefully and rely on APA standards and Bowen precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERPA 'eligible student' definition
rubrics_metrics.description: FERPA's implementing regulations define an 'eligible student' as a student who has reached 18 years of age or is attending an institution of postsecondary education (34 CFR 99.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining who has rights to inspect education records, institutions should apply this regulatory definition to distinguish parents from eligible students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology: prefer 'sexual interests' over 'sexual predisposition'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department views the term 'sexual interests' as more appropriate than the term 'sexual predisposition,' which the Department views as an outdated phrase that may conjure assumptions the Department seeks to prohibit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory text and institutional policies should favor modern, non-stigmatizing terminology (e.g., 'sexual interests') and avoid outdated phrases like 'sexual predisposition' except when quoting prior texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pregnancy-related protections and scope under PDA/EEOC view
rubrics_metrics.description: Some courts have held that PDA's protection of pregnancy-related medical conditions requires that those conditions be 'incapacitating,' but the EEOC in 2015 disagreed and the Department agrees the PDA contains no such limitation (citing cases and EEOC guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should not limit pregnancy-related protections to 'incapacitating' conditions; follow EEOC's broader interpretation and the Department's stated agreement when developing nondiscrimination policies and accommodations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory cost-estimation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's model estimates the total costs of the final regulations; many costs would be borne by recipients, some may be borne by others, and the model also accounts for non-required costs likely to be voluntarily borne by recipients or others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory impact analyses should separately identify mandatory compliance costs and likely voluntary costs, and describe allocation of costs across types of entities; this is the Department's approach in the preamble.
